lessons.title: Serial rules, parallel hardware
lessons.summary: A 4-bit counter. The hardware computes both next values at once; XBlue lets you read the cycle one rule at a time.
text: The hardware is parallel. In each clock cycle the counter computes both candidate next values at once, count + 1 and 0, and a multiplexer at the end picks one. Open the SystemVerilog tab: _t4 = _t3 ? (count + 1) : count is tick, and _t6 = _t5 ? 0 : _t4 is clear. Both data paths sit side by side.

XBlue reads it in order. schedule tick ≫ clear says: run tick, then run clear, which sees what tick wrote. A rule is atomic: its guard decides whether all of its writes happen. So the next count is two small steps, one after the other, not a priority between parallel paths.

One cycle, in order. Say count is 7, and enable and reset are both high. 1. tick runs: the counter is not full, so it writes 8. 2. clear runs, sees that 8, and overwrites it with 0. The count is 0: reset wins, and you never had to think about priority. At 15 it is shorter: 1. tick's guard is false, so it writes nothing. 2. With no reset, clear writes nothing either. The count stays 15.
The proof below states this story and Lean checks the design against it. interfaces is an implicit rule that drives every method output; it runs first.
try: Swap the schedule to clear ≫ tick. Read the rules in order and predict what a cycle with reset and enable both high does to the count. Then check the simulation: the reset is at cycle 20.
With enable always high and no reset after the start, predict what the count does once it reaches 15. Then check the simulation.

lessons.title: A pipeline FIFO: deq first, then enq
lessons.summary: One rule per side, run in order. A full FIFO takes an item in the cycle it hands one out.
text: The hardware. A FIFO that can enqueue and dequeue in the same cycle, even when full, needs a path from the dequeue side to the enqueue side: dequeuing frees a slot and enqueuing uses it at once. In the SystemVerilog tab, _t6 is count - 1 when the dequeue fires, and the enqueue's condition _t7 reads _t6, not count. The outputs (enq_ready, deq_valid, deq_data) are different: _t1 to _t3 look only at the registers.

XBlue reads it in order. schedule deq ≫ enq says: run deq, then enq, which sees what deq wrote. Each rule is atomic, and the guard is the handshake: deq fires when there is data and the consumer is ready, enq when there is room. The outputs are computed first, by the implicit interfaces rule, from the registers at the start of the cycle.

One cycle, in order. The FIFO is full (count = 2), and enq_valid and deq_ready are both high. 1. interfaces runs: enq_ready is count != 2 || deq_ready, which is true; deq_data is the oldest item. 2. deq runs: it fires, rp advances, count becomes 1. 3. enq runs and sees count = 1: it fires, writes the new item at wp, count becomes 2. 4. clear: no reset. The FIFO is full again, the old item went out and the new one came in. The simulation shows this at cycle 4.
The proof below states this story and Lean checks the design against it.
try: Make it a bypass FIFO. Change the schedule to enq ≫ deq and nothing else, and predict whether an item can enter and leave an empty FIFO in one cycle. Then also change the three outputs: enq_ready = count != 2, deq_valid = count != 0 || enq_valid, deq_data = count == 0 ? enq_data : data[rp]. Predict the empty-FIFO cycle again by reading the rules in order, then check cycle 2 of the simulation (an item is offered while the consumer is ready).
Keep the pipeline FIFO. With enq_valid and deq_ready both always high, predict how many items the FIFO holds in steady state and when deq_valid first goes high. Then check the simulation.
In the pipeline FIFO, change enq_ready to count != 2 (leave the rules alone). Predict what happens in the cycle where the FIFO is full, enq_valid is high and deq_ready is high. Then check cycle 4.

lessons.title: A round-robin arbiter
lessons.summary: Rotate, pick the first, rotate back: one block of logic in hardware, a short walk in order.
text: The hardware. Open the SystemVerilog tab. A round-robin arbiter is one block of combinational logic: a barrel shifter ({req, req} >> start, _s2), a priority mux over four bits that picks the first request, an adder that rotates the answer back (_s3), and a shifter that makes the one-hot grant (_t3). Why it is fair is not visible in the wires.

XBlue reads it in order. Most of the module is named values (Bit#(8) twice = {req, req};), recomputed where they are used; the only state is last. The cycle is three small steps: the implicit interfaces rule shows the grant computed from last, advance stores the winner, and clear runs last. The rotate trick is just how the hardware finds the first requester after last.

One cycle, in order. last is 1 and requesters 1 and 3 ask (req = 0b1010). 1. interfaces runs: start is last + 1 = 2. The scan goes 2, 3, 0, 1: requester 2 is not asking, requester 3 is, so the winner is 3 and the grant is 0b1000. 2. advance runs: last becomes 3. 3. clear: no reset. Next cycle the scan starts at 0 and finds requester 1, so the two requesters take turns. The last winner always goes to the back of the line.
The proof below states this story and Lean checks the design against it. priority case takes the first arm whose condition holds.
try: Set req to 0xf (all four request). Predict the winners from last = 3 by scanning in order, then check io_index in the simulation.
Set req to 5 (requesters 0 and 2). Predict who wins, cycle by cycle, starting from last = 3. Then check the simulation.
Make it a fixed-priority arbiter by replacing start with 0. Predict who wins with req = 0xf, and what happens to last. Then check the simulation and compare the gate count.

lessons.title: GCD: rules as an algorithm
lessons.summary: Euclid by subtraction. The rules chain, so one cycle can load, swap and subtract; each step sees the last.
text: The hardware is a chain. Because the schedule chains the rules with ≫, the emitted wires are a chain too. Open the SystemVerilog tab: _t5 is busy after finish, _t7 to _t9 are what load leaves, _t11 and _t12 what swap leaves, _t14 what subtract leaves, and _t16 is clear. Each stage reads the one before it.

XBlue reads it in order. Each rule is one step of Euclid's algorithm, guarded by when the step is legal: swap when x < y, subtract when x ≥ y, both only while y ≠ 0. A rule is atomic, and it sees what the earlier rules of the cycle wrote. So a cycle is five small steps in a fixed order, and a swap costs no extra cycle.

One cycle, in order. The unit is idle, start is high, a = 48 and b = 18 (cycle 1 of the simulation). 1. finish runs: not busy, nothing. 2. load runs: x = 48, y = 18, busy. 3. swap runs and sees them: 48 is not below 18, nothing. 4. subtract runs: 48 ≥ 18, so x = 30. 5. clear: nothing. At cycle 2 the registers are (30, 18): the load and the first subtraction happened in the same cycle. Two cycles later the cycle swaps and subtracts: (12, 18) becomes (18, 12), then (6, 12).
The proof below states this story and Lean checks the design against it.
try: Move subtract before swap in the schedule. Predict the first cycle in which io_done is high for gcd(48, 18) by tracing the registers in order, then check the simulation.
Predict the result and the cycle of io_done for the second job, gcd(105, 30), which starts at cycle 20. Trace it by hand in the original schedule, then check io_result.
Try swap ∥ subtract. Predict whether it is accepted, then compile it.

lessons.title: A pipelined multiplier
lessons.summary: Two stages, latest stage first: the rule order is what makes each register a pipeline boundary.
text: The hardware. Open the SystemVerilog tab. _t5 computes the next p from lo and hi, and _t8 and _t9 compute the next lo and hi from the inputs. All three are plain flip-flop inputs, side by side. Nothing in the wires says that p is a product, or when it appears.

XBlue reads it in order. A register written by one rule is visible to the rules after it in the same cycle. schedule stage2 ≫ stage1 puts the later stage first, so stage2 reads the old lo and hi before stage1 overwrites them. Each register is a pipeline boundary, and you read that off the schedule instead of finding it in the netlist.

One cycle, in order. Cycle 3 of the simulation: lo holds 56 (7 × 8 from the previous cycle) and the inputs are 255 and 255. 1. stage2 runs: p becomes lo + (hi << 4) = 56, from the old lo and hi. 2. stage1 runs: lo and hi become 255 × 15 each (the two nibbles of 255). 3. clear: nothing. So out_p is the product of the inputs from two cycles earlier. Gates shows the cost: two multipliers before optimisation.
The proof below states this story and Lean checks the design against it.
try: The stimulus feeds 3×4, 5×6, 7×8, then 255×255. Predict the cycle in which out_p shows 255 × 255 = 65025 (0xfe01), then check the simulation.
Swap to stage1 ≫ stage2. Predict the latency by reading the rules in order, then check when 3 × 4 = 12 appears on out_p.
Compute the whole product in one rule (p <= a16 * zeroExtend(in_b);). Predict the latency and what happens to the longest path, then check in the simulation and in Gates.

lessons.title: Cache-line state: reading the order finds the bug
lessons.summary: Valid / dirty bits for four lines, one operation per request. Reading the cycle in order shows why the writeback counter never moves.
text: The hardware. Open the SystemVerilog tab. Each op rule has its own chain of wires for valid and dirty: _t6 is the read miss, _t9 and _t10 the write, _t12 and _t13 the evict. The counter's enable _t14 is built from _t12 and _t13, not from the registers. In a page of wires that is easy to miss.

XBlue reads it in order. Each line goes Invalid → Clean (read miss) → Dirty (write) → Invalid (evict, with a writeback if dirty). The guards select exactly one op rule per request, and because three rules write valid they are chained with ≫. Every rule sees what the rules before it wrote, so countWb, the last in the chain, reads valid and dirty after evict.

One cycle, in order. Line 0 is valid and dirty, and the request is an evict of line 0 (cycle 2 of the simulation). 1. readMiss and write do nothing: wrong operation. 2. evict runs: the line is valid, so it clears valid and dirty. 3. countWb runs and asks whether the line is valid and dirty: evict just cleared both, so the guard is false. writebacks does not move. The output io_writeback, computed at the start, did go high, and the Simulation pane marks countWb as blocked (amber).
The proof below states this story and Lean checks the design against it.
try: In the simulation a dirty line is written back at cycles 2 and 4. By reading the rules in order, predict the value of writebacks afterwards, then check.
Fix the counter: move countWb before evict in the schedule. Predict writebacks at cycles 3 and 5, then check.
Add a flush op (req_op == 3) that clears every dirty bit. Predict io_dirty before and after the flush at cycle 3, then check.

lessons.title: Schedules decide throughput
lessons.summary: A 2-stage pipeline whose rate depends only on the order of ≫.
text: The hardware. Open the SystemVerilog tab. The three rules are a chain of wires: _t4 is v2 after drain; the exec guard _t5 reads _t4, not v2; the fetch guard _t9 reads _t8, the v1 that exec left. Reversing the schedule rewires the chain; no rule changes.

XBlue reads it in order. Each stage rule is guarded by its slot being free. With drain ≫ exec ≫ fetch, each rule sees the slot its successor freed in this cycle, so the rules can all fire in one cycle and the pipeline moves one item per cycle. With out_ready low, the guards alone stop each stage: no extra control logic.

One cycle, in order. Cycle 4 of the simulation: both stages are full (v1 and v2 set), s2 holds item 101, out_ready is high. 1. drain runs: the consumer takes item 101, v2 clears. 2. exec runs and sees v2 free: it moves s1 + 100 into s2 and clears v1. 3. fetch runs and sees v1 free: it loads next into s1. All three fired, and the pipeline is full again. When out_ready is low (cycles 14 to 17) drain's guard is false, so exec and fetch find their slots busy and nothing fires.
The proof below states this story and Lean checks the design against it.
try: Look at cycles 14 to 17, where out_ready is low. Read the rules in order and predict which rules fire. Then check the rule strip in the simulation.
Change the schedule to fetch ≫ exec ≫ drain ≫ clear. Predict, in order, what happens to a new item in one cycle, and whether out_valid is ever high. Then check the simulation.
Try (exec ∥ fetch). Predict whether it is accepted, then compile it.

lessons.title: Exercise: fix the credit counter
lessons.summary: Two bugs: the compiler finds the first; reading the rules in order finds the second.
text: A sender has 4 credits. take spends one per request, give returns one per response, and io_ok checks credits + inflight == 4: every credit is either here or out with a request. The hardware. Both rules change credits, so in hardware two candidate next values, credits - 1 and credits + 1, fight for one register. Rules in parallel (∥) would both read the same old credits and one update would be lost, so the front end refuses: that is the first error, on the schedule line.

XBlue reads it in order. With take ≫ give the two updates are serial: give sees what take wrote. In one cycle with a send and a response: credits 2, 2 in flight. 1. take runs: it fires, credits = 1, sent up by one. 2. give runs and sees the new sent: it fires, credits = 2, returned up by one. Credits and in-flight count are unchanged, as they should be.

The second bug is found the same way. Take the cycle where 4 requests are out, so credits is 0, and send is high. 1. take runs: its guard is inflight < 5, and 4 < 5, so it fires: credits = 0 - 1 wraps to 7 in 3 bits, and sent goes up. Now credits + inflight is 7 + 5 = 12, not 4. You do not need to find the cycle in a trace: read the guard with credits = 0.
try: First, it does not compile. The error is on the schedule line. Change it to take ≫ give ≫ clear, and predict, by reading the rules in order, what a cycle with both send and resp high does to credits. Then check cycle 10 of the simulation.
Predict the cycle in which io_ok drops, by reading take's guard when credits is 0. Then check the simulation, and fix the guard so that io_ok stays high.

lessons.title: A router's matrix arbiter
lessons.summary: From the CcNoc router: a priority matrix that gives the last winner the lowest priority.
text: The hardware. Each output port of the CcNoc router (XBlue/Examples/CcNoc/Router.lean) has an arbiter like this one, cut here to 3 requesters. Open the SystemVerilog tab: the grant is one expression over nine bits of pb and three request bits, and the new matrix, _t3, is nine more muxes that all depend on the winner. Why it is fair is not visible in the wires.

XBlue reads it in order. Bit 3*i+j of pb says requester i is above j; a requester wins when it asks and no asking requester is above it. permit and winner are functions over an Integer index: the front end unrolls them, so the hardware is plain gates. The cycle is two steps after the grant is shown: update moves the winner to the bottom (its row cleared, its column set), then clear runs last.

One cycle, in order. After reset pb = 0xee: 0 is above 1 and 2, and 1 is above 2. All three ask (req = 7). 1. interfaces runs: 1 and 2 are blocked by an asking requester above them, 0 is not blocked, so 0 wins (grant 1). 2. update runs: the row of 0 is cleared and its column set, so pb = 0xe8 and now 1 is above 0 and 2. 3. clear: no reset. Next cycle 1 wins, then 2: a requester that keeps asking loses to everyone who was waiting.
The proof below states this story and Lean checks the design against it. pb[k : k] <= v writes one bit.
try: Hold all three requests high (req = 7). Predict the first four grants from the order in the matrix, then check io_grant.
Hold only requesters 0 and 2 (req = 5). Predict which of them wins, cycle by cycle, then check.
Swap the schedule to clear ≫ update. Predict, in order, what pb is after a reset cycle in which requests are present, and compare with the original at cycle 10.

lessons.title: A blocking cache
lessons.summary: The shape of the CcNoc L2 slice: hits from the arrays, a miss walks a small state machine, and nothing else gets in until it is done.
text: The hardware. The CcNoc system's caches (stage 1, ported from Bluespec) are blocking: while a miss is being served, req_ready is low and nothing else gets in. This one has 4 lines of 8 bits. In the SystemVerilog the whole control state is one 2-bit register, and four enables read it side by side. Whether "nothing else gets in" is true depends on which copy of state each enable reads.

XBlue reads it in order. RegFiles are arrays: a read sees the start of the cycle, and an upd lands at the clock edge. The miss states are rules with exclusive guards on state, and the schedule runs them backwards, fill ≫ writeBack ≫ access, so each state lasts one cycle. A rule sees what earlier rules wrote, so access must not look at state where it runs: fill may just have set it to Ready. It uses req_ready, which interfaces computed from the state at the start of the cycle.

One miss, in order. At cycle 1 the cache is Ready and a request misses. 1. access latches the request and sets state to WriteBack. At cycle 2: req_ready is low; writeBack moves to Fill. At cycles 3 to 5 the cache waits in Fill (mem_fill high). At cycle 6 memory answers: 1. fill runs and sets state to Ready. 2. writeBack sees Ready: nothing. 3. access runs, but req_ready was low at the start of the cycle, so the request offered in this cycle is not taken. At cycle 7 req_ready is high again.
The proof below states this story and Lean checks the design against it.
try: Read the rules in order and predict the cycle in which the cache is ready again after the miss at cycle 1 (memory answers at cycle 6). Then check req_ready in the simulation.
Make access read state == 0 directly instead of req_ready. Predict, in order, what happens at cycle 6, when fill frees the cache while a request is offered. Then check cycle 7.
Reverse the schedule to access ≫ writeBack ≫ fill ≫ clear. Predict how a miss walks the states now, and check when mem_fill first goes high.

lessons.title: MSHRs: misses that do not block
lessons.summary: Two miss registers: hit-under-miss, miss-under-miss, secondary misses merged. Every new MSHR has a memory request behind it.
text: The hardware. Stage 2 of the CcNoc tutorial replaces the blocking L1 with a non-blocking one (L1NB.lean). Its heart is a small file of MSHRs: a miss takes a free one and asks memory; a load to a line that already has an MSHR waits on it (a secondary miss, merged: no second request); a hit is answered at once. In the SystemVerilog, the methods ld_ready and mem_req (_t1, _t4) look at mshr as it is at the start of the cycle, and the update is a separate chain of muxes. The two must agree about what the cycle did.

XBlue reads it in order. Reg#(Vector#(2, Mshr)) mshr is one register holding two structs; mshr[i] <= … writes one element and e with { f = v } updates one field. schedule load ≫ fill runs load on the MSHRs as the methods saw them, then fill frees the one memory answered. load either merges into the MSHR for its line or takes a free one.

One cycle, in order. Cycle 3: MSHRs 0 and 1 hold lines 3 and 5, a load to line 9 arrives, and memory answers MSHR 0. 1. interfaces runs: no free MSHR and no match, so ld_ready and mem_req are low. 2. load runs on the same MSHRs: neither matches, none is free, so it writes nothing. 3. fill runs: MSHR 0 becomes free. At cycle 4 the load is offered again: ld_ready and mem_req are high and it takes MSHR 0. Because load and the methods saw the same MSHRs, an MSHR is only taken when a request goes out.
The proof below states this story and Lean checks the design against it.
try: Give all loads the same line (ld_line = 3) and no fills. Predict how many requests go out and what secondary_misses does, then check mem_req in the simulation.
Make fill_valid always 0 and load three different lines, 3, 5 and 7. Predict what ld_ready does when the third arrives, by reading the rules in order, then check.
Swap the schedule to fill ≫ load ≫ clear. Predict, in order, what happens to the load of line 9 at cycle 3, and then check mem_req and the MSHRs at cycle 4.
